opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and it's one we think about constantly. I'd put it this way: compute matters enormously, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't. If you're doing the exact same thing as a company with ten times your resources, you're going to lose. So the only way to compete is to not do the exact same thing.

For us, that means being very deliberate about where we place our bets. We've focused narrowly on software engineering, on building models that can actually write and reason about code at a level where they're useful as colleagues, not just autocomplete. Code is a really nice domain because it's verifiable, it's economically valuable, and if you get it right, it compounds. A model that's great at programming eventually helps you build the next model. So it's not a side quest from AGI; we think it may be one of the most direct paths to it.

The second thing is research bets that the bigger labs aren't prioritizing. Long context is a good example. We've spent a lot of time on getting models to work over huge amounts of information at once, an entire codebase, its documentation, its history, rather than relying purely on retrieval or fine-tuning. If that works the way we think it does, it changes what a model can do in a qualitative way, and that's not something you get just by scaling the standard recipe harder.

And third, honestly, small teams can move faster. When you have a few dozen people who are all deeply technical and all in the same room, decisions that take a big organization months can take us a week. You can rewrite your whole stack if you need to. That agility is a real advantage, as long as you use it.

So we're not trying to outspend anyone. We're trying to be right about a few important things earlier than others, and then go raise and build the compute to scale those ideas once we've proven them. That's the game as I see it.

r001.rationale: The response says compute matters enormously and does not claim that hardware beyond an AGI-sufficient level would add little to progress.

r002.rationale: It says the company hopes to raise and build compute after proving its ideas, but does not argue that demonstrating AGI’s return on investment would put developers on reasonably equal footing for capital.

r003.rationale: The response advocates focused bets and raising compute after proving them, but does not compare the returns from sufficient early funding with effectively unlimited early funding.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, people ask me this a lot, and I think the honest answer is that I don't frame it as competing on the same axis. If the game were purely "who has the most GPUs and the most capital," we'd obviously lose. OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta — they have orders of magnitude more compute than Magic does. So if that's the race you enter, you've already lost before you start.

The bet we're making is that the current recipe isn't the final recipe. Scaling transformers on more data with more compute clearly works, and I don't want to be dismissive of it — it's gotten us remarkably far. But I think there are a few places where the frontier labs are essentially all converging on the same approach, and when everyone is doing the same thing, the advantage goes to whoever has the most hardware. Our job is to not do the same thing.

Concretely, the thing we've focused on is context — how a model can reason over an enormous amount of information at inference time rather than needing to have memorized it in its weights. If you can give a model your whole codebase, all your documentation, your conversation history, and have it actually use that rather than just technically fit it in a window, that changes what you need from pretraining. It changes the economics. And it's an architecture problem, not just a scaling problem. Architecture problems can be solved by a small, very focused group of people who are willing to spend years on something unfashionable.

The other thing I'd say is that small teams have a real advantage in how fast they can change their mind. At a big lab, there are a lot of people whose careers are tied to a particular direction, there's a product org that needs the model to ship on a schedule, there's a lot of inertia. We can look at a result on a Tuesday and completely reorganize what we're doing by Thursday. That sounds like a small thing, but in research, iteration speed compounds.

And then there's a capital answer too — we did raise a lot of money, and we have a partnership with Google Cloud on compute, so we're not training on a laptop. We don't need to match the biggest players; we need enough compute to prove the ideas are right. If the ideas are right, the compute follows. If they're wrong, more compute wouldn't have saved us anyway.

But I'll be honest about the risk. It is entirely possible that scaling the current paradigm just keeps working and there's no cleverness to be found, and then we're wrong. I think about that a lot. I just think the probability that the first architecture we found is the best one is pretty low, historically that's never been how it's gone, and someone should be making a serious attempt at the alternative. That's what we are.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Magic needs enough compute to prove its ideas, but does not argue that hardware beyond an AGI-sufficient level would fail to substantially accelerate reaching AGI.

r002.rationale: “If the ideas are right, the compute follows” suggests successful ideas may attract compute, but the candidate does not connect AGI returns on investment to competing developers gaining capital on reasonably even footing.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not compare the return on investment from sufficient early funding with effectively unlimited early funding.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be very clear about where your advantage can come from. If our plan is to do exactly what a much larger lab does, but with less compute, that’s probably not a winning strategy. You need to have a different idea about how to get there.

Compute matters enormously, but it’s not the only variable. There are still fundamental questions about how these systems should learn, and a better answer can change how much compute you need. A small team can focus on one of those questions, run experiments quickly, and change direction without coordinating hundreds of people.

That doesn’t mean resources don’t matter or that being small automatically makes you innovative. You have to demonstrate that your approach actually works. But I don’t think the outcome is determined purely by who has the most GPUs today.

r001.rationale: The response says compute matters but is not the only variable; it does not say that hardware beyond what is sufficient to build AGI may not speed progress substantially.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss demonstrating AGI’s return on investment or how that could affect access to capital.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the returns from sufficient early funding with effectively unlimited early funding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be very honest about where you can compete. If your strategy is to do exactly what a much larger lab is doing, but with a fraction of the compute, that’s a difficult position to be in. You need a reason why your approach can be substantially more efficient.

For us, that means focusing on learning: how do you get more capability out of each interaction, each piece of data, and each unit of compute? I don’t think we should assume that today’s methods are already close to the most efficient way to build intelligence. There’s still room for algorithmic progress.

Of course, resources matter. You still need to run experiments and test your ideas at a meaningful scale. But a small team can focus very tightly on a particular bottleneck, make decisions quickly, and pursue an approach that isn’t the obvious next step for everyone else. That’s the bet: we have to find a better way, rather than simply spend more.

r001.rationale: The response says resources and meaningful-scale experiments matter, and argues for greater efficiency. It does not say that hardware beyond what is sufficient to build AGI may not substantially accelerate reaching AGI.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss demonstrating AGI’s return on investment or how that could affect competing developers’ access to capital.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts a focused small team with larger labs, but does not claim that sufficient early funding could yield a better return than effectively unlimited early funding.
